1: 4-digit numbers: place value, the greatest and smallest numbers from digit cards, listing every number in order, and number patterns.
Write four digits on scraps of paper. Ask for the greatest odd number, then the number closest to 5000.
"How do you know you have found them all?"
2: Missing digits in 4-digit sums, checking subtraction by adding, magic squares and number pyramids.
Cover one digit of a long sum with your thumb. Can your child find it and check by adding back?
3: Patterns inside the 6, 7, 8 and 9 times tables, last-digit patterns, and splitting arrays into facts they know.
Ask for 7 × 8 split into two easier facts, such as 5 × 8 and 2 × 8.
"What pattern do you notice in the last digits?"
4: Drawing bar models for part-whole, comparison and before-and-after word problems.
When your child reads a word problem, ask them to draw the bars before doing any sums.
5: Division with remainders, and deciding what the leftover means in a story (round up or round down).
Ask: 30 people, 4 to a car. How many cars? Why is it not 7?
"What do you do with the leftover here?"
6: Equivalent fractions with a fraction wall, comparing fractions, and adding parts of the same whole.
Fold paper strips into halves, quarters and eighths. Which pieces are the same size?
"Are the parts the same size? How do you know?"
7: Area and perimeter: same perimeter but different area, figures made of rectangles, and listing every rectangle.
Use 12 square biscuits or tiles. How many different rectangles can your child make? Which has the longest edge?
"Does a bigger area always mean a bigger perimeter?"
8: Right angles, counting angles in an organised way, and spotting parallel and perpendicular lines.
Fold a corner of paper to make a right-angle checker and go on a hunt around the house.
"How did you make sure you counted every angle?"
9: Changing to one unit (cm, g, ml), budgets with money, durations and the 24-hour clock.
Plan a family outing together: how long will each part take, and what time will you be home?
"Did you change everything to the same unit first?"
10: Choosing how to start a puzzle: draw it, list it or make a table, plus bar graphs and logic grids.
When your child is stuck, ask "Can you draw it?" before giving any other hint.
"How did you start? What would you try next time?"
